name: PT Citra Nusantara Gemilang Tbk
industry_name: Gas & fuel distribution, refining and marketing

frontmatter.title: Citra Nusantara Gemilang - the trucked-gas network is worth more than the market pays
frontmatter.summary: Citra Nusantara Gemilang trucks compressed natural gas to Indonesian industry and retail where the pipeline does not reach. Nine-month profit already exceeds the whole of FY2025, free cash flow is negative while the LNG plant is built, and the shares trade below our DCF. We initiate at BUY on a target that holds the 2026 margin and prices the station programme, not a re-rating.
thesis: Nine-month net profit has overtaken the whole of the prior year on price, volume and the stations commissioned since 2025, and the shares have not re-rated.
The demand driver is structural rather than cyclical, as falling pipeline gas supply in West Java pushes industrial users onto trucked CNG [S6].
Retail is now a quarter of the customer portfolio and the station count is still rising, but the market capitalises the equity at a fraction of what the network is building [S3].
The risk is governance and liquidity, not the business - a thin free float, small turnover and a related-party gas supplier [S2].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results - whether the nine-month gross margin holds through the fourth quarter
Sumsel CNG station targeted to start operating, adding capacity in South Sumatra
Karawang LNG station commissioning, funded by the IPO proceeds earmarked for it

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Citra Nusantara Gemilang at BUY with a target of Rp158, 43.1% above the last price of Rp115. The company buys natural gas, compresses it and trucks it to industrial and retail customers in areas the pipeline does not reach - a small, capital-hungry distribution business that has just turned a corner. Nine-month 2026 revenue was IDR585.0bn and net profit IDR17.0bn; profit is already above the whole of FY2025, and revenue is running at an annualised pace above it [S0, S3].

The variant view is simple. The market treats the 2026 profit jump as a one-off in a microcap and capitalises the equity at 9.0x our FY2026 earnings and 3.9x EV/EBITDA on a FY2026E balance sheet that already carries the September net debt. Those multiples are not the argument: the like-for-like gas-distribution median is 7.7x and the pipeline incumbent, the closest comparable, trades nearer our level, so a re-rating is not what we are paid for. What we are paid for is the cash the station programme will produce after the build: our DCF is Rp142 a share against Rp136 from the multiple leg, and the target is their weighted value after the house liquidity discount. The jump we underwrite is the visible result of three things still in place - a structural shortfall of pipeline gas in West Java, the stations commissioned in 2025 and 2026 (Grobogan and Gresik in FY2025, Majalengka during 2026), and a retail book that now contributes a quarter of the customer portfolio [S2], [S3], [S4]. None of that reverses next year.

What moves the value: the FY2027 revenue path, which now rests on capacity that starts after 30 September 2026 - the Karawang LNG plant, half built at the last disclosure, and a first full design year from the 2025-vintage stations - not on a repeat of the 2025 commissioning; the gross margin, which is a pass-through contract margin rather than a spread bet; and the capex still to spend on the LNG plant, which the IPO proceeds already fund [S2], [S8]. The free cash flow is negative through the build and turns only when capex converges on depreciation; that is in the forecast, and the DCF is struck on it.

Trucked CNG is a niche inside Indonesian gas: it exists because the pipeline network reaches the
big industrial estates but not the smaller clusters, and a compressor station plus trailers is
cheaper than a spur line for volumes below a threshold. The business is therefore a toll on
logistics - the margin is the difference between the delivered gas price and the landed cost -
and it grows one station at a time.

CGAS sells and distributes natural gas, mostly as compressed natural gas, to industrial customers and, under its GASRA brand, to households and micro, small and medium enterprises; it also installs and services gas equipment and runs engineering, procurement and construction and operations contracts for CNG stations [S2]. Gas trading and distribution is the overwhelming majority of revenue, with the equipment and services book a small remainder [S2]. The revenue build shows the shape: the parent company booked IDR251.1bn of gas purchases and the subsidiaries a further IDR112.0bn against IDR505.3bn of consolidated cost of revenue in FY2025, so the company is fundamentally a reseller of gas through its own logistics [S2].

The distribution footprint runs through South Sumatra, West Java, Central Java and East Java, with stations and hubs at Cikarang, Waru, Palembang, Bandung, Klaten, Kediri, Malang and Lampung, the CNG stations at Gresik and Grobogan commissioned during FY2025 and Majalengka during 2026, and the Karawang LNG plant under construction [S2], [S4]. The Grobogan CNG station has a capacity of 1.5 MMSCFD [S2]. The group employed 314 people at the last count [S0].

The strategy the company states is expansion of distribution infrastructure, a stronger clean energy portfolio and operational efficiency [S2]. In practice that means stations and, now, LNG: on 5 May 2026 the company disclosed a plan to add an LNG business classification (a KBLI code) so it can process and handle LNG rather than only CNG, with shareholder approval to be sought at a shareholder meeting - no archived source evidences that resolution, so we treat the LNG mandate as planned rather than approved [S8]. The same disclosure carries the feasibility conclusion: an incremental net present value of IDR161.0bn from the LNG business, with the Karawang plant already 50.0% built [S8]. Management has also disclosed a new CNG station in South Sumatra, built by a subsidiary and targeted to operate in early 2027 [S6]. Capex for the Karawang LNG plant is funded from the IDR155.9bn of IPO proceeds earmarked for it, of which IDR13.1bn of project costs and IDR35.0bn of asset advances were already on the balance sheet at the end of FY2025 [S2].

Ownership is concentrated and family-linked: PT Petro Asia Energy holds 32.3% of the shares, PT Dharma Mulia Jaya a further stake, and the register holds other private vehicles, leaving 29.8% in public hands [S2]. The shares listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2024 and the count stands at 1,771 m shares [S2]. There is no conglomerate parent behind the company: the controlling holders are private vehicles, which is why the governance overlay in section six matters more than a group story would. CGAS is a challenger in its industry rather than the leader - the pipeline operator and its affiliates dominate the larger industrial volumes - but it is an incumbent in the trucked niche, with permits, land and customer relationships built since 2005 [S2].

Indonesian gas demand is served two ways: by pipeline, largely for the big industrial estates and power, and by trucked or liquefied gas for everyone the pipeline does not reach. CGAS sits in the second. Its 2026 demand driver was explicit in the company statement accompanying the third quarter: sales grew on higher average selling prices and volumes and on the full use of capacity after the new stations started, while rising industrial demand was reinforced by a fall in gas supply through the pipeline network in West Java [S6]. The company's own wording for the revenue growth is a rise in the average selling price as well as in volume [S4], so this is not a pure volume story: part of the growth is price, and the thesis depends on the margin being retained through it. What is structural is the re-routing of industrial fuel demand created by infrastructure, and it is the single most important fact here. The company itself lists the pipeline shortfall as one of the two reasons industrial demand reached it this year [S4].

Policy cuts both ways. The government administers the gas price for certain industrial users, and in 2026 it cut the price of LNG for the industrial sector to US$13.0/MMBtu, valid to the end of the year [S7]. Cheap LNG is a competing fuel for the same industrial customer, and it also caps what a distributor can charge on top of its own landed cost. For CGAS the regulatory risk is therefore a margin risk rather than a volume risk: the administered price does not remove the customer's incentive to switch away from diesel or from pipeline gas, but it limits the spread the distributor earns on the switch.

Competition comes from the pipeline operator and its affiliates wherever the network reaches, from other CNG and LNG distributors, and from alternative fuels - diesel, LPG, kerosene and the subsidised electricity grid. The barriers are permits, land for stations and hubs, gas supply contracts and the capital to build, and the company describes its industry as requiring large investment, carrying high risk and dependent on uncertain gas supply, with competitor expansion into distribution named as a share risk [S2]. CGAS's edge is tenure and permits in the trucked niche; its disadvantage is scale, a single product family and a balance sheet that can fund one large project at a time.

We score the five forces as follows. Supplier power is high: gas comes from a handful of upstream sellers, and the main related-party supplier, PT Bayu Buana Gemilang, sold IDR236.3bn of gas in FY2024 - just under half of that year's revenue - falling to IDR40.6bn in FY2025, under a tenth of revenue [S2]. The collapse of that line is treated in section three, because it coincides with the margin expansion and is not explained in the accounts. Buyer power is moderate: the customer base is industrial and retail and diversified enough that no single counterparty dominates, and the retail brand now contributes a quarter of the customer portfolio [S3]. The threat of new entrants is moderate - the capital is not large by Indonesian standards but the permits and the gas contracts take time - and substitutes are real, because pipeline gas is cheaper wherever it exists. Rivalry is local and price-led, and the moat, such as it is, is a permit-and-contract moat rather than a cost moat.

The commodity deck matters only through cost. Brent sets the reference path for the gas purchase price, and our model carries 71.9% of cost of revenue exposed to it with complete pass-through in the base case, on the evidence of 2026 rather than by assumption: the deck puts Brent well above its FY2025 average for FY2026, yet the nine-month gross margin rose [S0]. Full pass-through is the single assumption that carries the margin, not a footnote, so the bear case runs it a sixth short of full and the reported margin path under partial pass-through is in section five. CGAS is not a price-taker on a commodity; it is a margin-taker on a contracted spread. The one structural weakness of the model is that the spread is thin - gross profit was IDR106.6bn on IDR611.9bn of revenue in FY2025, so a single point of margin is worth a large share of operating profit [S2].

FY2025 revenue was IDR611.9bn, up from IDR508.5bn in FY2024, with gross profit of IDR106.6bn and operating income of IDR22.1bn [S2]. Net profit attributable to shareholders was IDR14.2bn and the return on equity 5.5% [S2]. The 2026 run-rate is materially better: revenue of IDR585.0bn in the first nine months and net profit of IDR17.0bn, with the company describing the profit as up by roughly four fifths year on year and revenue up by a third [S6]. Note the comparison the press release uses: it measures the nine-month profit against a prior-year nine-month figure, while the audited FY2025 attributable profit was IDR14.2bn [S2]. We use the audited accounts.

The cost structure is a purchase-and-resell book. Gas purchases are the great majority of cost of revenue - IDR251.1bn at the parent plus IDR112.0bn in the subsidiaries against IDR505.3bn of consolidated cost of revenue [S2]. Overhead and direct labour make up most of the rest, and depreciation the remainder. Our forecast holds the nine-month 2026 gross margin of 18.7% through FY2028E and shades it to 18.5% by FY2030E as retail grows and the LNG station starts at a lower initial utilisation, with 18.0% long-run. Operating expenses take IDR84.5bn of the FY2025 revenue, and we hold that ratio broadly flat, which is the conservative side of the operating leverage the company showed this year [S0].

Depreciation is where the data pack is wrong and we restate it. The fixed-asset note of the audited accounts charges IDR16.6bn in total for FY2025, split between cost of revenue and administrative expenses, and IDR12.4bn in FY2024, while the data pack's D&A line carries a fraction of that because it misses the depreciation charged inside the subsidiaries' cost of revenue [S2]. On the restated numbers FY2025 EBITDA is IDR38.7bn and the EBITDA margin 6.3%. The same correction lifts FY2024 EBITDA to IDR19.1bn, which is why the historical margin in our table is higher than the one the pack reported.

Cash flow is the weak spot and we do not dress it. Free cash flow to the firm was negative in both of the last two audited years - FY2024 on IDR46.5bn of capex and FY2025 because capex plus the working-capital build exceeded the cash the business generated - and the size of the outflow is in the summary table [S0]. The audited cash-flow statement puts FY2025 operating cash flow at IDR12.2bn against IDR15.9bn of net profit, so cash conversion was positive but below accounting profit; the gap is about one per cent of assets once the project spend is stripped out, which is not an accruals warning [S2]. Our forecast keeps free cash flow negative through the build: IDR-35.6bn in FY2026 on IDR62.7bn of capex and a working-capital build of IDR25.5bn, and capex falling from IDR66.8bn in the heavy LNG year to IDR50.0bn by FY2030E [S2]. The turn comes when capex converges on depreciation, not before.

Working capital is the number the model had to be rebuilt around. On a basis that excludes project spend, operating working capital for FY2025 is IDR79.2bn, rather than the fifth of revenue the data pack reports, because a large part of the pack's figure is project spend rather than the gas book: prepaid costs on the Karawang LNG plant of IDR13.1bn and asset-purchase advances of IDR35.0bn are capital spending carried in current assets [S2]. We therefore hold working capital at the ex-project ratio of 12.9% of revenue on both the opening and the forecast balance, which is IDR79.2bn against IDR611.9bn in FY2025. On that basis FY2026E absorbs IDR25.5bn of working capital as revenue grows, not releases it; the project spend itself sits in the FY2026E capex line, so it is counted once.

The balance sheet at the end of FY2025 held IDR55.1bn of cash against IDR38.9bn of debt, a net cash position [S0]. By 30 September 2026 the drawdown had taken the company from net cash to net debt, with bank lines funding the LNG build [S0]. The engine charges interest on opening balances, so the FY2026E line of IDR3.7bn understates the year: the charge on the September debt, with the nine-month actual already in the accounts, is carried in other non-operating items (IDR-9.0bn) rather than left out. On the actual debt the FY2026E net profit is IDR22.5bn, below the company's IDR23.9bn target rather than above it, and the DPS follows at Rp6. Capital allocation is simple: a fifty per cent payout, with IDR4.7bn paid in FY2025 from the FY2024 profit and the FY2025 dividend of Rp4 a share paid in mid-2026, and the rest into stations [S2]. No rights issue, placement or buyback is outstanding, and we assume the share count stays at 1,771 m shares [S2].

Earnings quality: the accruals test does not flag the name. Operating cash flow of IDR12.2bn in FY2025 against IDR15.9bn of net profit is a small gap, but it was produced only after a working-capital build that the Karawang project advance explains only in part. Three items we do flag. First, receivables: trade receivables rose from IDR47.9bn to IDR65.3bn and other receivables from IDR1.5bn to IDR8.7bn, faster than revenue - so receivable days lengthened - and by more than the year's operating cash flow [S2]. Receivables grew well ahead of revenue - the house divergence test is one and a half times - and it is an optics-class flag: the balances are disclosed and audited and the customers are industrial accounts, but a distributor whose receivables outrun its sales is either extending credit to hold volume or booking revenue it has not collected, and the accounts do not let us tell which. The DSO move belongs in the risk premium until the FY2026 accounts show collection. Second, the related-party purchase line: IDR236.3bn of gas was bought from PT Bayu Buana Gemilang in FY2024, just under half of that year's revenue, and IDR40.6bn in FY2025, under a tenth - a collapse of that size in the year the gross margin rose from 16.1% to 17.4% is not explained anywhere in the accounts, and it is the single largest unexplained item in the earnings history [S2]. It is optics-class rather than manipulation-class: the flow is disclosed, audited and priced at arm's length on the face of it, but it is exactly the channel through which value leaks in Indonesian small caps, and we would want the FY2026 accounts to show where that volume went. The annual report's statement that there were no material conflict-of-interest transactions is made in the IPO use-of-proceeds report, not as a general representation on related-party trade, so we do not read it as contradicting the purchase line [S2]. Third, the company's own growth narrative in the press and the MD&A does not always reconcile to the audited line items, so we build the model from the accounts and the balance sheet rather than from commentary.

We value CGAS on discounted free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, cross-checked against EV/EBITDA. That fits a business whose value is the station and hub build: the cash flows are project-level, the asset base is long-lived, and the earnings multiple the market pays for a microcap is a reading of sentiment as much as of value. The weights are 70% DCF and 30% EV/EBITDA, with the dividend-yield leg set to zero - a departure from the industry default that we set out below.

The cost of capital is built from the sovereign and the industry beta: a risk-free rate of 7.4% less the 1.6% default spread the engine applies to the Indonesian sovereign, the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.80 levered to 1.05 at the observed debt-to-equity ratio of 0.41 and the statutory tax rate of 22.0%. That gives a cost of equity of 13.9% after a 1.0% premium for size, and a WACC of 12.0%. The debt leg is 9.4% pre-tax, the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread, and it is the only cost of debt in the model: the interest line charges the same 9.4% on opening balances, so the P&L and the discount rate use one rate. That rate is the observed marginal cost, not the data pack's interest-over-year-end-debt ratio, which reads higher only because the balance moved - from IDR21.4bn at the end of FY2024 to IDR38.9bn at the end of FY2025 and then to the September drawdown. Against average debt, the FY2025 charge of IDR2.6bn is below this rate, and the nine-month 2026 gross charge on the drawn balance is close to it; the FY2026 opening-balance shortfall is carried in other non-operating items, so the year still bears the actual interest [S0, S2]. Liquidity is charged once, not twice: the size premium is one point, and the illiquidity charge is the 10.0% the house applies to the probability-weighted value, because three-month turnover is about IDR504.2m against a market capitalisation of IDR203.7bn and a holder cannot build or exit a position without moving the price [S0]. The target is shown before and after that discount: Rp176 weighted, Rp158 after it.

The DCF produces Rp142 a share on an enterprise value of IDR307.8bn, of which 67.3% is terminal value. The explicit forecast carries revenue from IDR808.9bn in FY2026 to IDR1,316.6bn in FY2030, an EBITDA margin from 8.0% to 8.5%, capex falling from 7.8% of revenue in the 2026 build year to 3.8% by FY2030E, and terminal growth of 4.5%. The sensitivity to the terminal capex assumption is the largest single risk to the number: charging growth capex forever at the build rate, on a terminal growth rate below it, would value the company at a fraction of the figure above, which is why capex converges on depreciation rather than staying at the construction rate [S2].

The cross-check now agrees with the DCF, and the earlier gap was composition, not only depreciation. The EV/EBITDA leg is Rp136 a share at 7.7x, -4.2% against the DCF. The multiple is the median of a like-for-like set - the pipeline and distribution incumbent, the gas-infrastructure builder and the fuel distributor-retailer - not the industry-wide median, which was pulled to double digits by four shipping names whose asset intensity has nothing to do with a trucked-gas network [S0]. Two further corrections matter: the multiple is applied to trailing FY2025A restated EBITDA, not to a forecast year, so the metric year is disclosed and the leg is not a forward multiple in disguise; and the peer data packs carry the same D&A understatement we restated at CGAS, which biases their multiples high, so we keep the leg at a cross-check weight rather than letting it anchor the target. On price-relative multiples the stock is not obviously cheap against the pipeline incumbent, which trades at a similar EV/EBITDA; that is why the call rests on the DCF and not on a re-rating [S0].

The dividend-yield leg, which the industry default weights at fifteen per cent, is set to zero for two reasons. The first is that capitalising next-twelve-month DPS of Rp6 at the peer median yield produces a value several times the DCF, which no minority holder in a company with a 29.8% free float could realise: the house card requires a yield valuation to clear the sovereign with a spread rather than to match a peer yield. The second is that on that test CGAS does not clear it. At Rp115 the forecast dividend of 5.5% is below the ten-year government yield of 7.4% - the spread is negative, not positive - so the shares fail the yield-versus-sovereign hurdle and the total return of 43.1% is capital appreciation to the target, not income [S0]. Ownership here is a bet on the station programme compounding, not on the dividend.

The card's other cross-check is the AFFO yield, and that one passes. AFFO is EBITDA less maintenance capex, cash interest and cash tax. Our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR64.3bn less the depreciation charge of IDR22.2bn, which we use as the maintenance-capex proxy because the company splits no maintenance from growth spend and capex converges on that charge once the build ends, less cash interest of IDR3.7bn and cash tax of IDR9.3bn leaves an AFFO that, over the market capitalisation of IDR203.7bn, yields well above the ten-year government yield of 7.4%; the spread survives charging the September bank debt in full rather than only the opening balance the interest line carries. The negative free cash flow in the financial analysis is not AFFO: it is growth, the IDR62.7bn of total capex against IDR22.2bn of maintenance and a working-capital build of IDR25.5bn. That distinction is why this is not duration risk wearing an equity costume: the cash, before the build, clears the sovereign [S0, S2].

What does today's price imply? At Rp115 the equity sits above the bear-case value of Rp41 and below the base-case value of Rp140, so the market is not capitalising the base case and is giving some, not no, credit to the station programme. The scenario table carries two columns and they are not interchangeable: the today-value column is the fundamental value today if that scenario holds, and the rolled column is the value twelve months out, which is what the target machinery uses. The probability-weighted average of the three rolled values - Rp154 base, Rp47 bear and Rp349 bull at weights of 50.0%, 25.0% and 25.0% - is Rp176, and the target of Rp158 is that figure after the 10.0% liquidity discount. A reader can rebuild the target from those three numbers. To get to our value an investor needs the 2026 gross margin to hold as the new stations run a full year, which is what the nine-month accounts show, and the Karawang LNG plant to commission on schedule, which the IPO funding makes plausible [S2], [S6]. At 3.9x EV/EBITDA on our FY2026E EBITDA and 9.0x on our FY2026E earnings, on FY2026E figures that include the bank debt drawn for the build, the price is consistent with treating the current profit as a peak; the record and the station pipeline say it is not [S0].

The largest downside is demand reversal. If pipeline gas returns to West Java in volume, the industrial customers who switched to trucked CNG switch back, and the growth we capitalise disappears. Likelihood: medium over three years, because the shortfall is an infrastructure and supply fact rather than a price one [S6]. Impact: high - this is the thesis, and it is the reason the bear case is credible rather than decorative.

Gas supply and contract risk is next. The company depends on a small number of suppliers and on purchase agreements being renewed, and its annual report names uncertain gas availability as a core industry risk [S2]. Related-party supply concentration adds a governance dimension, because the main related-party supplier was a large fraction of purchases two years ago and a much smaller one in FY2025 [S2]. Likelihood: medium; impact: high, on both volume and margin.

Regulatory and price risk: the industrial gas price is administered, and the reduced LNG price for industry of US$13.0/MMBtu runs only to the end of 2026 [S7]. A change in the administered price or in the LNG compensation scheme can compress the spread CGAS earns on a fixed volume, and because the LNG plant's outlet price after 2026 is not set, the revenue line that the 2027 capex peak buys rests on a price basis that expires before the plant starts. Likelihood: medium; impact: medium on the base, high on the LNG leg.

Contract and feedstock risk: the Karawang plant's supply is a DRAFT gas sale agreement with Pertamina EP - the feasibility file lists it as a draft agreement and a ministry allocation letter dated 4 July 2025, with a contract period running from 1 June 2026 to 30 November 2033 [S8]. A draft is not a contract: if the terms are not executed, the plant that absorbs the largest capital commitment in the plan has no feedstock and the IDR13.1bn and IDR35.0bn of sunk project spend are impaired. That is why the plant is valued only through its own forecast cash flow and the sunk spend is carried at the balance-sheet value, not added as a separate item. Likelihood: low to medium; impact: high on the asset, medium on the group.

Project and execution risk: the Karawang LNG plant is the biggest single capital commitment, it is funded from IPO proceeds, 50.0% built at the last disclosure, and it is the asset that has to change the revenue mix [S2], [S8]. A delay or cost overrun defers revenue, consumes cash and would leave the company holding prepayments and advances rather than a working asset. Likelihood: medium; impact: medium.

Financial risk: the company moved from net cash at the end of FY2025 to net debt during 2026, and free cash flow was negative in both of the last two audited years [S0]. A funding need at the wrong moment would be met with expensive short-term bank debt, at a cash cost the model carries at 9.4% on the opening balance - the same rate used to discount the DCF, so a refinancing shock raises both the charge and the hurdle rather than flattering either. Likelihood: low to medium; impact: medium.

Governance and liquidity risk: a closely held register, a free float of 29.8% and a related-party supplier [S2]. Our cost of equity carries a premium for this. A narrowing of the governance discount is part of the bull case and a widening of it is the bear case, and at this market capitalisation of IDR203.7bn a single holder's decision moves the price more than any operating line. Likelihood: structural; impact: high on the multiple.

Probabilities are 50.0% base, 25.0% bear and 25.0% bull. The bear is the demand reversal implemented, not described: ten points off the growth rate every year, which takes FY2027 growth to high single digits and turns revenue negative by FY2030E; two points off the gross margin, which gives back the 2026 gain and more; half a point of extra capex for a delayed project; and pass-through a sixth short of full, so that share of the oil-linked gas cost is absorbed. The bull is the same drivers on the other side - ten points on growth, which carries the Sumsel station in the first quarter and an early Karawang commissioning, and half a point less capex - but only one point on the margin, because the base of 18.7% already contains the 2026 gain and the third quarter was the best quarter in the record; pass-through stays at the base level, since an administered price and a competing LNG benchmark cap how far a spread can widen. The asymmetry is deliberate and sourced, and it is the honest direction: a distributor with one year of elevated margin has more room to give it back than to add to it. The bear value of Rp41 is well below the price, so the market is not pricing the reversal we describe as a quarter-probability event; the bull value of Rp314 needs the pipeline shortfall to persist, the LNG plant to commission and Sumsel to start, and it is not what the target assumes.

Signposts that would change our view: a recovery in West Java pipeline supply; a gross margin below the FY2025 level for two consecutive quarters; a cost overrun or delay at Karawang; a change in the administered industrial gas price; the Sumsel station slipping out of early 2027; and any related-party transaction that becomes material relative to revenue [S6], [S7].

Control sits with private vehicles - PT Petro Asia Energy at 32.3% of the shares, PT Dharma Mulia Jaya, PT Cipta Nyata Gemilang and PT Tirta Maritim Nusantara - with a free float of 29.8% [S2]. The founders and the controlling holders are the same people who run the company, which is normal for an Indonesian small cap but means minority interests depend on their discipline. No pledge of controlling shares is disclosed in the annual report and we found none in the material we archived; the absence of a disclosure is not proof, but it is the best evidence available at this size.

Related-party dealings are the item to watch. Gas was purchased from PT Bayu Buana Gemilang, a related party, at IDR236.3bn in FY2024 - just under half of that year's revenue - and IDR40.6bn in FY2025, under a tenth [S2]. The company has a standing disclosure regime for material and affiliated transactions, and the filing we cite for it is the 2022 disclosure of that regime rather than a statement about FY2025 [S9]. The annual report's sentence that there were no material conflict-of-interest transactions in the period sits in the IPO use-of-proceeds report, so we read it as a representation about the offering, not as a general statement on related-party trade [S2]. The purchase line and the margin move together and neither is explained; we treat it as an optics-class flag rather than a manipulation flag, because the flow is disclosed and audited and the accounts are clean on cash, but it is a channel through which value can leak, and it belongs in the risk premium rather than in a footnote.

The second optics-class flag is receivables. Trade receivables rose from IDR47.9bn at the end of FY2024 to IDR65.3bn at the end of FY2025, and other receivables from IDR1.5bn to IDR8.7bn, both faster than revenue, so the collection cycle stretched even as the customer base was said to be shifting to retail [S2]. A longer DSO is not evidence of fabricated sales at this size, but it is the first place a working-capital squeeze would show, and it means the earnings are not yet fully backed by cash. We carry it as an optics-class flag in the risk premium and would want the FY2026 trade-receivables ageing to confirm the balances are with the industrial accounts rather than with affiliates.

The auditor issued an unqualified opinion on the consolidated accounts, and there has been no auditor down-tier change in the period we reviewed [S2]. The dividend record is short but consistent: a fifty per cent payout, paid every year since listing, with IDR4.7bn paid in FY2025 from the FY2024 profit and Rp4 a share paid in mid-2026 from FY2025 [S2]. The company states no fixed ratio, only that it pays when retained earnings are positive, so the payout is a policy of the controlling holders rather than a commitment.

On ESG, the product is part of the transition case - natural gas substitutes for diesel and heavy fuel oil in industrial heat and transport, with lower local emissions - and the company's own reporting leans on that. The offsetting exposures are safety at compressor stations and on gas trailers and the upstream methane footprint of the gas it buys, neither of which the company quantifies in the material we reviewed [S2]. The board and the audit function are small, as at most issuers of this size, and the governance work falls to the annual report and the shareholder meeting rather than to independent committees.

The FY2026 audited results, expected in the first quarter of 2027, are the first test of whether the nine-month IDR17.0bn of net profit holds through the fourth quarter [S6]. The company's June 2026 public expose set a revenue target of IDR879.0bn and a net profit target of IDR23.9bn for FY2026 [S5]; our forecast is IDR808.9bn of revenue, below the revenue target because reaching it would need a fourth quarter well above the third, and IDR22.5bn of net profit, below the target because the interest on the September debt is a cost the target predates.

The company's own feasibility work is the bull cross-check we do not put in the base. Management's projections to 2033 underpin an incremental net present value for the LNG business of IDR161.0bn, and the Karawang plant was 50.0% built when that case was published [S8]. That is a project value, not an equity value, and it is contingent on a draft gas sale agreement being executed; it is why the bull case, not the base, carries Sumsel and an early Karawang commissioning.

The Sumsel CNG station, targeted to operate in early 2027, is the next operating catalyst because it adds a province and a customer base rather than capacity at an existing hub [S6]. The Karawang LNG plant is the structural one: commissioning converts the prepayments and advances already on the balance sheet - IDR13.1bn and IDR35.0bn [S2] - into revenue-generating assets, and is the point at which the LNG leg becomes measurable rather than promised.

Between updates we monitor four KPIs: station throughput and the number of stations in service; the gross margin, which should stay at or above the FY2025 level if pass-through is working; capex against the IPO allocation of IDR155.9bn [S2]; and the related-party purchase line, which should stay small and be explained rather than simply shrink. We also watch share turnover, because at current liquidity a change in the register would matter more than a change in the business, and the execution of the Karawang gas sale agreement, which is the condition on the sunk spend.

bear.narrative: West Java pipeline gas returns in volume and the industrial switch to CNG reverses; the new stations ramp at half pace; the Karawang LNG station slips a year, so the growth rate falls by ten points a year and FY2027-FY2030 growth is close to nil; the 18.7% gross margin gives back the 2026 gain as competitors meet the retail price, and complete pass-through fails so a fifth of the oil-linked gas cost is absorbed. Capex rises because a delayed project is a more expensive project.

bull.narrative: The pipeline shortfall in West Java persists, industrial and retail customers keep switching to CNG, the Karawang LNG plant (already half built) commissions early and the Sumsel station starts in the first quarter, adding a province; throughput at the 2025-vintage stations reaches design, lifting growth by ten points a year, and the margin holds the third quarter's level rather than reverting. Pass-through stays at the base 1.0: the administered industrial price and the US$13/MMBtu LNG benchmark cap how far the spread can widen, so the bull upside is volume, not a higher spread.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +32.2% is the nine-month actual of Rp585.35bn (F21) plus a fourth quarter of Rp223.7bn, which is Q3-2026's Rp211.0bn grown 6% for the year-end industrial pull that lifted Q4-2025 to Rp185.2bn from Rp161.2bn in Q3-2025 [S0]. That lands FY2026 at Rp809bn, below the Rp879bn public-expose target (F24) because reaching it would need a Rp294bn fourth quarter after a Rp211bn third. FY2027E +18.0% comes from capacity that only starts after 30 September 2026: the Karawang LNG plant (50% built at the 5 May 2026 disclosure, F35, construction funded from the Rp155.9bn IPO allocation, F20) commissioning during 2027, a first full year at design throughput from the 2025-vintage stations at Gresik (2 MMSCFD) and Grobogan (1.5 MMSCFD), which the annual report says started operating in FY2025 [S2 p.31], and Majalengka (1 MMSCFD) running through its first full year after starting in 2026 [S2 p.53]. It is a ramp, not a new full year: the 2025 stations' benefit is already in the 9M2026 actual. Sumsel (early 2027, S6) is held for the bull case, not the base. FY2028E-30E 14%/11%/9% decelerate as the station pipeline thins; the 4.5% terminal rate is below the house 5.29% real GDP path because a gas distributor cannot outgrow the industrial base it serves [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 18.7% is the nine-month 2026 actual: gross profit Rp109.5bn on revenue Rp585.4bn (three quarterly gross profits of Rp32.2bn, Rp37.2bn and Rp40.2bn) [S0]. It is above the FY2025 17.4% (F4 over F1) because the mix moved to retail (25% of the customer portfolio, F23) and the new stations ran fuller. Margins are held at 18.7% to FY2028E and shaded to 18.5% by FY2030E as retail grows and the LNG station starts at a lower initial utilisation; 18.0% long-run. The 30.29% gross-profit growth of FY2025 (F28) shows the direction of travel, not a repeatable rate.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Gas purchases of Rp251.11bn at the parent (F12) plus Rp112.00bn in the subsidiaries (F13) are Rp363.11bn of the Rp505.34bn cost of revenue (F3), 71.9%. The rest is overhead, direct labour, project equipment and depreciation, none of it oil-linked.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Complete pass-through, on the evidence rather than by assumption: the deck prices Brent at US$96 for FY2026 against a FY2025 average of US$68, yet the nine-month 2026 gross margin rose to 18.7% from 17.4% in FY2025 [S0] - the gas purchase contracts and the selling prices reset together, and the ASP increase is what the company itself cites for the 37% revenue growth [S3]. A partial pass-through would build a margin collapse into FY2026 that the actual accounts contradict. The link is kept at 72% of COGS so the exposure is declared and re-tested in the bear case [S2].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 operating expenses were Rp79.11bn on Rp585.35bn of revenue, 13.5% [S0], against 15.2% on the three-year average and 13.8% in FY2025 (F5 over F1): revenue grew 32% while costs grew 7%, so the fixed base of 314 group employees is being spread. Held at 13.5% and shaded down to 13.2% by FY2030E, stopping short of assuming further leverage.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the fixed-asset note, not the data pack: total depreciation was Rp16.61bn in FY2025 (F9) and Rp12.37bn in FY2024 (F10), against the pack's Rp4.76bn and Rp2.38bn, because the pack misses the depreciation charged inside the subsidiaries' cost of revenue. That is 2.71% of FY2025 revenue, rising to 3.0-3.2% as the LNG station and the 2025 CNG stations enter service [S2].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 7.75% is statement capex of 4.6% of revenue - the nine-month 2026 spend of Rp25.3bn with a fourth quarter at the Q4-2025 pace of Rp11.7bn, Rp37.0bn in total, which is exactly the twelve-month capex line in the data pack [S0] - plus Rp25.7bn of project cash actually paid in 2026 through prepaid project costs and asset advances (the 2026 movement in F18 and F19, implied by the 30 September cash balance), which the cash-flow statement carries below capex. The fourth quarter is not given a step-up: no filing or archived disclosure gives a 2026 capex plan above the run-rate, so the statement line is the twelve-month actual and not a number solved back from the cash roll. FY2027E 7.0% carries the heaviest remaining LNG construction year, funded from the Rp155.9bn of IPO proceeds earmarked for the station and equipment (F20); the Rp48.1bn already sunk at 31 December 2025 (F18 + F19) is on the FY2025 balance sheet and is not spent twice in the forecast. FY2028E-30E fall to 5.0%, 4.0% and 3.8% as the build ends, converging on the 3.0-3.2% depreciation rate so that the terminal year is not charged growth capex forever on a 4.5% growth rate; 3.5% long-run. The FY2025 actual was 5.8% of revenue [S2].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 12.94%, the FY2025 ratio on a basis that excludes the Karawang LNG project spend: operating working capital is Rp79.19bn (F29) against revenue of Rp611.90bn (F1), because the Rp13.11bn of prepaid project costs (F18) and the Rp35.02bn of asset-purchase advances (F19) are capital spending carried in current assets, not the gas book's working capital, and the same treatment is applied to FY2024 (F30, F33). Holding one ratio across the forecast keeps the cash-flow line consistent: the project spend sits in the FY2026E capex line, so it is not counted twice, and no reclassification release is booked in FY2026E. On the pack's unadjusted 20.8% the build would double-count project spend; on the pack's 12.26% three-year average the first forecast year would book a Rp28bn release that is only the prepayment leaving working capital [S2].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A; FY2025 effective rate was 28.0% on pre-tax profit of Rp22.08bn (F6)

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 9.45%, the sovereign plus the house corporate spread - the same rate the WACC uses, so one borrowing cost is applied throughout. It is the observed marginal rate, not the pack's mechanical interest-over-year-end-debt ratio of 11.09%: that ratio divides by a balance that moved during the year, so FY2025 interest of Rp2.60bn against average debt of Rp30.15bn (Rp21.37bn opening, Rp38.89bn closing) is 8.6%, and the 2026 quarterly statements show Rp4.50bn of interest over nine months on average gross debt of Rp60.84bn, 9.9% annualised, with the third quarter alone at 8.7% [S0]. The observed range therefore brackets 9.45%; the FY2026 opening-balance charge is topped up in other_nonop so the year still carries the actual nine-month interest, and from FY2027 the drawn balance is charged at this rate [S0].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +Rp43.9bn: total debt rose from Rp38.89bn at 31 December 2025 (F-notes, bank loans Rp33.01bn plus consumer financing Rp5.88bn) to Rp82.79bn at 30 September 2026, a Rp43.90bn drawdown in the nine months, which is the actual financing of the Karawang build and the working-capital build of the third quarter [S0]. From FY2027E zero: the remaining station spend comes from the Rp155.9bn IPO allocation (F20) and operating cash, and the book repaid bank debt in every year of the audited record [S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E Rp-9.0bn, in two disclosed parts. Rp-3.0bn is other charges below operating profit: the nine-month 2026 accounts carry about Rp3.5bn of them (pre-tax profit Rp23.2bn against operating profit Rp30.4bn and net interest of Rp3.8bn) [S0], and the FY2025 line was Rp-0.2bn. The further Rp-6.0bn is the interest the engine's opening-balance convention misses: it charges 9.45% on 31 December 2025 debt of Rp38.89bn (about Rp3.7bn gross), but the September balance sheet carries Rp82.79bn, so the nine-month actual net interest of about Rp3.8bn plus a fourth quarter on the drawn balance is about Rp5.8bn net against net interest income of about Rp0.2bn on the opening-balance line. Carrying the difference here keeps FY2026E net profit on the actual debt; FY2027E onward the opening balance is the September debt (net_borrowing FY2026E), so the line reverts to the other-charges run-rate. [S0]

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A; minorities took 10.5% of FY2025 net profit (Rp1.67bn of Rp15.88bn, F8)

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 50% is the observed policy, not a default: Rp4.706bn was paid from the FY2024 profit (F17), 50.0% of the Rp9.412bn attributable profit (F7), and Rp4.00 a share was paid in June 2026 from FY2025, 49.9% of the Rp8.024 EPS [S0]. The AR states no fixed ratio, only that cash dividends are paid when retained earnings are positive [S2].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: no rights issue, placement or buyback is announced; 1,771.5m shares at 31 Dec 2025 (F16)

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.5%: Indonesian nominal gas-distribution growth, above the 3.3% world growth the AR cites for 2026 but below the house 5.29% real GDP path, because a CNG distributor's terminal volume is the industrial base it has already connected [S2].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E FCFF of +Rp36.3bn, the line that turns the story, is produced by delta_nwc of -Rp28.2bn, a working-capital release in a year revenue grows 32%, after builds of +Rp60.3bn (FY2024A) and +Rp58.2bn (FY2025A). The model's nwc_pct is 12.26% against FY2025's actual 20.8% (NWC Rp127.3bn). Section 3 states the model 'keeps the pack's ratio ... that is the conservative treatment', the opposite of what fund record does. On the consistent ex-LNG-prepayment ratio of 12.9% ((127.3-48.1)/611.9), FY2026E delta_nwc is about +Rp25bn and FCFF about -Rp17bn, not +Rp36bn.
challenges.answer: Working capital restated on a consistent ex-LNG basis: FY2025 nwc facts F29 (Rp79.19bn) and FY2024 F30 (Rp55.71bn) exclude the prepaid project costs F18 and the asset-purchase advances F19, and nwc_pct is held at 12.94% on both the opening and forecast balance, so FY2026E delta_nwc is +Rp25.5bn and FCFF -Rp17.4bn instead of +Rp36.3bn; the DCF re-ran at Rp168 and section 3 now states the treatment it actually uses [S2].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E np_parent of Rp26.2bn sits 9.5% above the company's own Rp23.9bn target on a model net interest charge of Rp0.46bn, below the Rp3.8bn of net interest the analyst says was already incurred in 9M2026, and with debt frozen at Rp38.9bn while the 30 September 2026 balance sheet shows Rp82.8bn debt and Rp42.0bn cash. On actual debt, net interest is about Rp6.2bn and np_parent about Rp22bn, below guidance rather than above it.
challenges.answer: FY2026E rebuilt from the September balance sheet: net_borrowing +Rp43.9bn reflects the debt drawdown, the interest the opening-balance convention misses is carried in other non-operating items, and np_parent falls to Rp22.8bn, below the company's Rp23.9bn target rather than above it; DPS follows at Rp6 and section 7 now says below [S0].

challenges.challenge: The Rp230 EV/EBITDA leg applies the 10.71x peer median to FY2025A trailing EBITDA (metric 38.71, not forward) and to CGAS's restated EBITDA, while the report says peer multiples are computed on data-pack EBITDA that understates depreciation: applying an inflated multiple to an inflated EBITDA double-counts. The peer set is not like-for-like either: GTSI 41.9x, HITS 17.1x, SHIP 14.5x, HUMI 13.2x are shipping names; PGAS, the only gas distributor, is 3.66x, on which the leg is about Rp76 a share, not Rp230.
challenges.answer: Peer set replaced with like-for-like gas distributors and downstream marketers (PGAS, RAJA, AKRA), the metric year is stated as trailing FY2025A restated EBITDA, and the multiple falls to 7.7x so the leg is Rp159, -5% against the DCF rather than +40%; the composition and D&A biases are both disclosed in section 4 [S0].

challenges.challenge: The 2.7x EV/EBITDA quoted twice in section 4 and in the extreme_call justification is computed with the model's FY2026E net CASH of Rp42.1bn, while the 30 September 2026 balance sheet the analyst cites shows net DEBT of Rp40.7bn. EV at the current price is about Rp259bn, or about 4.0x FY2026E EBITDA, not 2.7x. At 4.0x against PGAS at 3.66x the 'cheap on multiples' claim largely disappears.
challenges.answer: Every price-relative multiple is recomputed on the model balance sheet that now includes the Rp43.9bn drawn by September: FY2026E EV/EBITDA is 3.6x, not 2.7x, in line with PGAS rather than cheap, and the sentences and the extreme-call justification use the placeholder and state that the call rests on the DCF, not a re-rating [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative (revenue growth halves, stations ramp at half pace, LNG station slips a year) is not implemented by the shocks, which are -4pp a year growth, -1.5pp gross margin and +0.5pp capex. The bear still grows 28% in FY2026 and 14% in FY2027, and its 17.2% margin only reverts to FY2025's 17.4%, while the bull adds 1.5pp to 20.2%, above anything in the record (FY2024 16.1%, FY2025 17.4%). The asymmetry runs the wrong way for a risk section that rates demand reversal 'impact: high'.
challenges.answer: The bear now implements its narrative: ten points off growth a year, two points off the gross margin (below FY2025), half a point of extra capex and pass-through of 0.85, which takes the bear value to Rp48; the bull margin is one point, sourced to the third quarter's 19.0% actual, and the asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications [S3, S2].

challenges.challenge: There is no downside to pass-through anywhere in the model: link1_pass is 1.0 in base, bear and bull, so 71.9% of COGS carries no cost risk and the oil deck is inert. Section 2 asserts the 2026 growth is 'not a price effect', but the cited source S4 says growth was driven by 'kenaikan harga jual rata-rata dan volume penjualan' (higher ASP as well as volume). In an administered-price regime, the pass-through evidenced by one year of margin is the central assumption, not a footnote.
challenges.answer: Pass-through is now shocked in the bear at 0.85 with the cap at full pass-through in the bull, justified in qc_justifications, and section 2 no longer claims the growth is not a price effect: it cites the company's own wording, higher ASP as well as volume [S4, S7].

challenges.challenge: The Karawang LNG feedstock is a DRAFT agreement with Pertamina EP and a draft GSA (S8 pages 5-7, 'draft perjanjian'), while the Rp48.1bn prepayment and advance is added to the bridge at probability 1.0 and the US$13/MMBtu industrial LNG price that governs the outlet runs only to 31 December 2026 (S7). Section 5 lists delay and overrun but not the unsigned supply or the price basis of the asset that the 2027 capex peak buys.
challenges.answer: The Karawang feedstock is stated as a DRAFT gas sale agreement with Pertamina EP plus a ministry allocation letter of 4 July 2025, in section 5 and in post_bs_review, the bridge is probability-weighted to 0.85 instead of 1.0, and the industrial LNG price expiring at end-2026 is a named risk [S8, S7].

challenges.challenge: Related-party gas purchases fall from Rp236.3bn (46% of FY2024 revenue) to Rp40.6bn (6.6% of FY2025) with no explanation, exactly as gross margin rises 16.1% to 17.4% to 18.7%; the report treats it as an optics footnote and never discloses the prior-year percentage. Separately, 'operating cash flow has exceeded net profit' contradicts the model's own FY2025A FCFF of -Rp61.1bn, implying operating cash flow of about -Rp26bn after a Rp58.2bn working-capital build; and the 'no material conflict of interest' sentence is from the IPO use-of-proceeds report (S2 page 92), not a general RPT representation.
challenges.answer: The related-party collapse is now disclosed with both years (just under half of FY2024 revenue to under a tenth in FY2025) against the margin move, the earnings-quality conclusion rests on audited operating cash flow of Rp12.2bn against Rp15.9bn of net profit, and the conflict-of-interest sentence is cited to the IPO use-of-proceeds report [S2].

challenges.challenge: The published scenarios cannot produce the target. Sections 4 and 5 print bear Rp103 and bull Rp313 (v0 values) while the target machinery uses Rp114 and Rp350; 50% x 204 plus 25% x 103 plus 25% x 313 = 206, and 206 x (1 - 10%) = Rp185, not Rp196. A reader cannot reproduce the target from the numbers shown, and the 'price is at the bear case' line changes meaning with which set is used.
challenges.answer: One scenario reconciliation in section 4: v0 (value today) and rolled values are distinguished, the three rolled values at their weights give the weighted value of Rp199 and the target of Rp179 is that figure after the 10% discount, so a reader can reproduce it [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2027E +18% growth is attributed to 'the two 2025 stations (Grobogan, Majalengka, Gresik) running a full year', but the AR (S2 page 31) says Gresik and Grobogan started operating IN FY2025, so their full-year effect is already inside the 9M2026 actual, and S4 says the new stations operated 'sepanjang 2026'. On that timing FY2027 gets a ramp, not a new full year. The basis also calls three stations 'two', and Majalengka's status differs between S2 page 31 and S2 page 53.
challenges.answer: FY2027 growth is re-based on capacity starting after 30 September 2026 - Karawang commissioning and a first full design year from the 2025-vintage Gresik and Grobogan stations - with each station's date sourced; the two-station error and the Majalengka inconsistency are removed [S2, S6].

challenges.challenge: Upside the analyst owns is left out of the model: the Sumsel CNG station (early 2027, S6) is called the next operating catalyst in section 7 but is absent from the FY2027 growth build; the Karawang plant is already 50% built (S8 page 5) yet completion progress is never used; the company's Rp879bn revenue target is 8.7% above the model's Rp809bn; and management's own 2026-2033 projections sit in S8 unused as a bull cross-check.
challenges.answer: Sumsel and early Karawang commissioning are carried in the bull only, and the company's own feasibility case - incremental NPV of Rp161bn and the plant 50% built - is cited in section 7 as the cross-check the base does not take [S8].

challenges.challenge: cov_engine qc reports FY2025A calibration at 6.33% actual versus 7.95% model (gap 1.62pp) with no qc_justification, and weights.changed still shows justified false because the argument sits in valuation.weights_note rather than qc_justifications. The section 4 cost-of-equity paragraph also omits the -1.62pp default-spread deduction the engine applies, so the stated inputs (7.45% rf, 1.05 beta, 6.7% ERP plus CRP, 2.0% premium) give about 16.4%, not 14.9%.
challenges.answer: qc_justifications now carry the calibration drift and the weights change with sources, and the cost-of-equity paragraph publishes the 1.6% default-spread deduction alongside the risk-free rate, ERP, CRP and beta [S3, S0].

challenges.challenge: Source hygiene: S2, S3, S4, S5 and S8 carry no dates; S9 is a 2022-09-29 filing cited for the current RPT regime. Section 1 says the June 2026 RUPS 'approved' the new KBLI, but S8 is the pre-RUPS feasibility disclosure ('rencana penambahan KBLI', RUPS 'rencananya' June 2026) and no archived source evidences the resolution. The three-station list is cited to S2 and S6 though S4 is the source, and the mid-2026 dividend was Rp7.1bn (Rp4.00 x 1,771.5m, +51% on Rp4.7bn), not 'a similar amount'.
challenges.answer: Sources are dated where the text evidences a date (S4 4 November 2026, S5 public expose 15 June 2026, S8 5 May 2026) with a note where it does not, the KBLI addition is restated as planned not approved, and the dividend and station citations are corrected [S8, S4, S5].

challenges.challenge: Two liquidity charges and a zeroed leg stack against the target: a 2.0% size and illiquidity premium inside a 14.9% cost of equity (the 'one judgement' in the build), then a further 10% liquidity discount on the probability-weighted value, and the 15% dividend-yield leg set to zero although the shares yield 6.4% against a 7.4% sovereign. Each is argued separately but they are neither netted nor tested.
challenges.answer: One liquidity treatment: the cost-of-equity premium is cut to 1.0% as a size premium and illiquidity is charged once through the house discount, with the target shown both before and after it (Rp199 weighted, Rp179 after), and the zeroed yield leg is explained against the sovereign yield [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E statement capex of ~Rp44.5bn is unsourced: the stated derivation (9M2026 spend of Rp25.3bn plus a Q4 at the Q4-2025 pace of Rp11.7bn) gives Rp37.0bn, leaving a ~Rp7.5bn gap that flows straight into FY2026E FCFF (~+Rp7.5bn) and the DCF, so the target is not reproducible from the sources.
challenges.answer: FY2026E statement capex reset to Rp37.0bn, the pack twelve-month capex line (9M2026 Rp25.3bn plus a Q4 at the Q4-2025 pace of Rp11.7bn); the unsourced Rp7.5bn is removed, total FY2026E capex is Rp62.7bn (7.75% of revenue) after the Rp25.7bn of sourced project cash, FCFF moves to -35.6 and the engine re-derived the target [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states that the 5.5% dividend yield against the 7.4% 10-year FR spread "is the reason the dividend is worth having", but that spread is negative (-1.9pp), and the report omits the AFFO-yield cross-check against the 10y FR required by VAL_INFRA_TOWERS_TELCO.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now says the forecast yield of 5.5% against the 7.4% ten-year is a negative spread that fails the sovereign hurdle, with the total return sourced to capital appreciation; the mandatory AFFO cross-check (EBITDA less the depreciation charge as maintenance capex, cash interest and cash tax) is added and clears the ten-year, and negative FCFF is attributed to growth capex and working capital [S0, S2].
